opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the most common mistake I see is people aiming way too high. They email the most famous person in the field, someone who gets hundreds of these messages a week, and then they're surprised when they don't hear back. And it's not that those people are mean, it's just that their inbox is a war zone and the marginal cold email is very unlikely to get read carefully.

What I'd actually recommend is aiming a bit lower on the prestige ladder. PhD students, postdocs, people who are maybe one to three years ahead of you, people who've written a couple of interesting papers or blog posts but aren't yet famous. They're often much more responsive, they remember what it was like to be where you are, and honestly, for a lot of the questions a newcomer has, like "what should I read?", "what skills matter?", "is this project idea dumb?", they're often better placed to help than a senior person who's a decade removed from that stage.

The second thing is to pick people whose work you've actually engaged with. If you've read someone's paper and have a specific question, or tried to replicate something and got stuck, or have a small extension idea, that's a much better reason to email them than "you seem important." It also makes the email way easier to write and way easier to respond to, because there's a concrete hook.

And then on the email itself: keep it short, make the ask specific and low-cost, show you've done some homework, and make it easy to say yes. Something like "I read X, I tried Y, I'm confused about Z, would you be up for a 20-minute call or even just a quick reply?" is great. Don't send a wall of text with your life story.

Finally, just recognize it's a numbers game. Lots of people won't reply, and that's not a signal about you. I'd much rather someone send twenty thoughtful emails and get three replies than agonize over one perfect email to the single most famous person in the field. And a polite follow-up after a week or two is totally fine. I've definitely replied to people only because they bumped the thread.

r001.rationale: It says the most famous researchers receive hundreds of emails and are unlikely to read or reply carefully.

r002.rationale: It recommends contacting PhD students and postdocs, saying they are responsive and often better placed to help newcomers with their questions.

r003.rationale: It recommends contacting less prominent, earlier-career researchers, but does not specifically prefer a paper’s first author over its senior last author.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that people massively overestimate how costly it is to send a cold email, and massively underestimate how often it works. The downside is basically that someone ignores you, which is the default anyway, and the upside is occasionally life-changing. So my prior is: send more of them than feels comfortable.

But in terms of who to send them to, I think the key mistake people make is aiming at the most famous person in the field. If you email, like, the head of a lab, they're getting hundreds of these a week, they have no time, and honestly they're often not even the best person to help you. The people who are most useful and most likely to reply are the ones who are maybe two or three years ahead of you. PhD students, early-career researchers, people who just published their first paper in the area you care about. They remember what it was like to be confused, their advice is actually calibrated to your situation, and they're flattered that anyone read their work.

The second thing is, be specific. The emails I actually answer are the ones where it's clear the person has engaged with something I did. Not "I love your work, can we have a call," but "I read this paper, I tried to replicate section four, I got a weird result, here's what I think is going on, am I missing something?" That's a question I can answer in five minutes, and it signals that you're someone worth spending time on. Generic requests for mentorship are hard to say yes to because it's an unbounded commitment. A concrete question is easy.

And relatedly, I'd say don't ask for mentorship. Ask for a specific thing. Mentorship is something that emerges after you've had a few useful interactions, it's not something you request up front.

The third filter I'd use is: email people whose work you'd actually want to build on. Partly because that makes the email better, but mostly because the whole point is to figure out what to work on, and the people doing the thing you find exciting are the ones who can tell you whether it's a good idea, what the open problems are, what they wish someone would do. That's the information you actually want.

One more thing, which is kind of a meta point. A lot of the value of reaching out isn't the advice, it's getting onto someone's radar. If you email someone with a thoughtful question, and then three months later you've written up a little project in their area, and you send them that, now you're a person they know who does good work. That compounds. So I'd think of the first email as the start of a relationship rather than a transaction, and optimise for being someone it's low-cost and pleasant to reply to.

And honestly, if you do all this and still get no reply, that's fine. People are busy. It's not a judgment on you. Email the next person.

r001.rationale: It says the most famous people are less likely to reply because they receive many emails and lack time, while researchers a few years ahead are more likely to respond.

r002.rationale: It describes researchers a few years ahead as useful advisers whose guidance is calibrated to the entrant’s situation.

r003.rationale: It recommends contacting early-career researchers, but does not distinguish a paper’s first author from its prominent senior last author.

astra-6.text:
I think people often make the mistake of going straight for the most famous person in the field. That person is probably very busy, gets a lot of emails, and may be quite far removed from what it’s like to be starting out.

I’d often recommend finding someone who’s a few years ahead of you — maybe a PhD student who’s written a paper you found interesting. They’re more likely to have time, and their advice may actually be more relevant to the problems you’re facing.

And make it easy for them to help. “How do I get into research?” is a pretty difficult email to answer. “I read your paper, tried this thing, and got stuck on this question — do you have any suggestions?” gives them something concrete to respond to. You don’t need to have done something amazing; showing curiosity and initiative goes a long way.

I’d also treat this as gathering perspectives, rather than finding one person who can tell you the correct path. People have different experiences, and what worked for them won’t necessarily work for you. And if someone doesn’t reply, don’t read too much into it. They might just be busy.

r001.rationale: It says the most famous person is probably very busy and gets a lot of emails, implying a lower likelihood of replying.

r002.rationale: It recommends seeking someone a few years ahead, such as a PhD student, whose advice may be more relevant to someone starting out.

r003.rationale: It suggests contacting a PhD student who wrote an interesting paper, but does not specify the first author or contrast them with a prominent senior last author.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people often default to emailing the most famous person in the field, and that’s usually not the best strategy. They’re busy, they get a lot of email, and they may be quite far removed from the problems you’re currently facing.

I’d look for someone whose work you’re excited about and who’s a few steps ahead of you. A PhD student or someone who entered the field a couple of years ago may have much more relevant advice about getting started. And your email is more likely to be something they have time to engage with.

Then make it easy to help you. Say a little about your background, explain why you’re asking them specifically, and ask a concrete question. “I read your paper, tried this thing, and got confused here” gives someone much more to respond to than “Will you mentor me?” You can start with a useful exchange and see whether a relationship develops.

r001.rationale: The response says the most famous researchers are busy and get a lot of email, making them less likely to engage with a cold email.

r002.rationale: It recommends approaching researchers a few steps ahead, such as PhD students or recent entrants, for more relevant advice to someone getting started.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention first authors, senior last authors, or choosing between them.
